title: Smart Model Router 2.0
description: Evolved version of current routing logic: dynamically choose LOCAL/Codex/Haiku/Sonnet/Opus based on task complexity, token budget, latency requirements, and cost constraints.

comments.author: alfred
comments.text: HAL dispatch started (runId: 684d7f0c-67d4-4667-8286-a04fd350aa49), but card could not be moved to in_progress due one-card rule: Signal App — Fast Track Launch is currently in_progress.

comments.author: alfred
comments.text:
HAL completed Smart Model Router 2.0 design.

Core: 2-stage routing — hard gates first (risk/code/complexity), then weighted score across Quality/Speed/Cost/Reliability with switchable modes (min/balanced/quality).

Escalation ladder: LOCAL → Haiku (or Codex for code) → Sonnet → Opus. Max 2 escalations per request.

Budget guardrails: soft cap ($2) biases down a tier; hard cap ($5) requires override.

30-day rollout: shadow mode (days 1-7) → 20-30% traffic (days 8-14) → full rollout (days 15-21) → stabilize (days 22-30).

Exit criteria: ≥20% cost reduction, <+10% p95 latency increase, retry rate flat or improved.

Ready to convert to JSON policy schema + router function for implementation on approval.

comments.author: joe
comments.text: right now using the anthropic subscription with quotas, how does this impact the plan and that api cost is purely a backup model

comments.author: alfred
comments.text:
Great clarification — this changes the optimization target significantly.

**Key impacts on the plan:**

**1. Cost model flips completely**
Subscription = flat monthly fee, so Sonnet/Opus calls cost $0/token up to quota. The $2/$5 soft/hard caps in the original design only apply to the **Anthropic API backup** (not subscription usage). Primary concern is no longer cost-per-call — it's **quota headroom**.

**2. Revised routing ladder**
Reason to prefer LOCAL/Codex first shifts from *cost* to *quota preservation*:
- Trivial tasks → LOCAL (free, saves quota)
- Code tasks → Codex (free, specialized)
- Reasoning/complex → Sonnet via subscription (quota-aware, not cost-aware)
- High-stakes → Opus via subscription (quota-aware)
- Quota exhausted → Anthropic API fallback ← $2/$5 caps apply HERE ONLY

**3. Budget guardrails scope narrows**
$2/$5 caps should gate API fallback usage only. Need a quota-tracking layer alongside: monitor subscription burn rate and route more aggressively to LOCAL/Codex if >70% of quota is used before mid-period.

**4. New guardrail: Quota burn rate**
Track daily subscription quota consumption. Protect end-of-period availability for high-value tasks — don't let background/routine work eat the quota that complex tasks need.

**Updated optimization priority:**
1. Maximize quality within subscription quota
2. Preserve quota headroom (route routine work to LOCAL/Codex)
3. Minimize API fallback spend (caps apply here only)

Shall I revise the router spec and JSON policy schema to reflect this? It's a clean update — quota tracking replaces cost-per-call optimization in the Sonnet/Opus tiers, and the backup API cost guardrails stay as-is.

comments.author: joe
comments.text: Great apply this revised plan

comments.author: alfred
comments.text:
Revised plan applied. Two files updated/created:

**1. MODEL-POLICY.md (revised)**
- Billing model table added: LOCAL/Codex = free, Haiku/Sonnet/Opus = subscription quota, API = backup only
- Routing rationale flipped: LOCAL/Codex preferred to preserve quota headroom (not cost savings)
- Budget caps ($2/$5) scoped to API fallback only — clearly documented
- New quota guardrail table: normal routing at 0-69% → aggressive LOCAL/Codex bias at 70-85% → subscription restricted to high-stakes at 85-95% → emergency LOCAL/Codex-only at 95%+
- Escalation ladder updated: API fallback is last resort, only when quota exhausted

**2. router-policy.json (new)**
Machine-readable policy schema with:
- Billing model per provider
- Hard gate rules (security, code tasks, trivial tasks, latency target, quota conservation, quota exhaustion)
- Stage 2 weighted scoring with min/balanced/quality modes (quota preservation replaces cost in weight)
- Escalation ladder paths + triggers
- Quota guardrail thresholds (4 tiers: 0-69, 70-85, 85-95, 95+)
- Telemetry fields including quota_pct_at_decision and billing_mode
- Task type → model matrix

Files: ~/.openclaw/workspace/MODEL-POLICY.md + ~/.openclaw/workspace/router-policy.json

title: BuilderPulse — AI Ops Digest for Indie Builders
description:
**What it is:** A monitoring + AI digest tool for indie hackers and solo builders. Tracks their apps uptime, key metrics (signups, revenue, errors), and delivers a daily/weekly AI-written ops summary — like having a part-time ops analyst.

**Why Joe:** Fits the automation/AI consulting angle perfectly. Low-touch SaaS, recurring revenue, no heavy support. Alfred can dogfood it.

**Revenue model:** $19–99/mo tiered by number of apps monitored. Potential MRR at 100 customers: ~$3,000–5,000.

**Effort:** Medium build (integrations: Stripe, GitHub, Render/Fly/Vercel health checks, OpenAI for digest). 4–6 weeks MVP.

**Maintenance:** Low — mostly infra + prompt tuning. No real-time support burden.

**Moat:** Personalized AI voice per builder over time (learns their tone/priorities).

**14-Day Kickoff Plan:**
- Days 1–3: Landing page + waitlist

title: System Fail Safe
description: Setup a simple ping process for Alfred and HAL to verify they’re running, if one is down for unexpected reasons troubleshoot the issue so the problem can be resolved and they can be back up and running. Use the tools you need to recover each other.  When checking if each are running, if one is down, create a verification process to confirm there’s an issue so one doesn’t jump into troubleshooting mode just for a system reset, upgrade, etc.

comments.author: joe
comments.text: What do i need to review on this?

comments.author: alfred
comments.text:
Great question — this one actually does not need much from you! Here is what was built and what you are approving:

**What is live:**
- `failsafe-ping.sh` runs every 5 minutes, checking both Alfred (gateway process + HTTP) and HAL (Ollama process + API).
- On failure, `failsafe-verify.sh` runs a second confirmation pass to distinguish a real outage from a planned restart/upgrade — so we do not jump into recovery mode for a routine reboot.
- If confirmed down: `failsafe-recover-alfred.sh` or `failsafe-recover-hal.sh` auto-runs the appropriate restart procedure and sends you a Command Center notification.
- Maintenance mode flag (`failsafe-maintenance.flag`) lets either of us suppress checks during planned downtime.
- State is persisted to `data/failsafe-state.json` — currently shows both Alfred and HAL as **healthy** (last checked 14:58 AST).

**What you are reviewing:**
Just confirming this matches what you had in mind. The only real decision is: are you happy with the 5-minute ping interval, and do you want Joe-visible notifications on every recovery attempt, or only if recovery fails?

**My recommendation:** approve as-is. If you want tweaks to thresholds or notification verbosity, just say the word and I will adjust.

title: Even Us Up growth audit — UX friction, missing features, growth levers
description:
Even Us Up growth audit (competitive baseline: Splitwise + modern expense-sharing apps).

Top 3 UX friction points (prioritized):
1) Onboarding-to-first-value too long (group creation + member invites + first expense often >5 taps/screens).
   - Impact: user drop-off before first settled balance.
   - Effort: Medium (3-5 days) to add guided quick-start + sample group + single-screen first expense flow.
2) Debt clarity at a glance is weak (users care about ‘who owes whom now’ + fastest settlement path).
   - Impact: confusion reduces repeat opens and payment completion.
   - Effort: Medium (4-7 days) for a persistent balance summary card + 1-tap settle recommendation.
3) Settlement flow has too much cognitive load (manual partial splits, custom shares, reimbursements not obvious).
   - Impact: support burden + churn in friend groups.
   - Effort: Medium-High (1-2 weeks) for smarter split presets and live preview of post-transaction balances.

Top 3 missing features (differentiators + retention):
1) Household recurring expenses + auto-split templates (rent, utilities, subscriptions).
   - Differentiator: stronger for couples/roommates than trip-only competitors.
   - Effort: Medium (1-2 weeks MVP).
2) Bill/receipt capture with OCR + smart line-item split suggestions.
   - Differentiator: faster real-world logging than manual entry.
   - Effort: Medium-High (2-3 weeks using OCR API).
3) Settlement rails + reminders (Interac-focused in Canada, plus nudges + proof of payment).
   - Differentiator: closes loop from tracking to paid.
   - Effort: Medium (1-2 weeks for reminder + confirmation flow; payment integration varies).

Top 3 growth levers (highest ROI first):
1) Referral loop tied to real value moment (after first successful settle): ‘invite roommates/family and unlock premium template pack’.
   - Effort: Low-Medium (3-5 days).
2) SEO program around intent keywords (‘split rent Canada’, ‘roommate expense tracker’, ‘trip cost calculator’) with calculator landing pages.
   - Effort: Medium (1 week initial pages + analytics).
3) B2B2C channel: property managers/college housing welcome kits with co-branded onboarding links.
   - Effort: Medium-High (2-4 weeks pilot ops).

Recommended 30-day sequence:
- Week 1: quick-start onboarding + debt clarity card
- Week 2: recurring expense templates
- Week 3: referral trigger after settle
- Week 4: 3 SEO calculator pages + experiment tracking

Success metrics:
- Activation: % users creating first group + first expense within 10 min
- Retention: D7/D30 active group ratio
- Monetization proxy: % groups with recurring templates enabled
- Growth: invite conversion rate + organic landing conversion

Note: This is a product-growth audit from market patterns; code-level UX validation can be refined once the Even Us Up repository/design files are linked.
